title: Human body
summary: An adult human is a single organism built from about 30 trillion human cells organized into tissues, organs and eleven cooperating organ systems.

layers.basics: Your body is a layered machine. Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs team up in organ systems that move you, feed you, protect you and think.
layers.deeper: Roughly 60% of adult body mass is water. The systems constantly trade signals and materials: the nervous and endocrine systems coordinate, the cardiovascular system delivers, and the skin, kidneys and lungs keep the internal environment stable (homeostasis).
layers.expert: Typical reference adult: about 30-40 trillion human cells and a comparable number of resident microbes (roughly 1:1, not the old 10:1). Core temperature is regulated near 37 C, plasma pH near 7.40, and blood glucose near 5 mmol/L through negative-feedback loops.

did_you_know: You shed roughly 30,000-40,000 dead skin cells every minute, and most of the dust on a table is not mostly skin.

title: Integumentary system
summary: The skin and its hair, nails and glands form a waterproof, self-repairing outer barrier.

layers.basics: Your skin keeps water in and germs out, helps control temperature through sweat, and lets you feel touch. Hair and nails are made of tough keratin.
layers.deeper: The skin is the body's largest organ. Its layers (epidermis, dermis, hypodermis) house sensory receptors, sweat and oil glands, hair follicles, and a vascular network that can shunt blood to shed or hold heat. It also makes vitamin D3 when UVB reaches the epidermis.
layers.expert: Barrier function depends on the stratum corneum 'bricks and mortar' of corneocytes and lamellar lipids (ceramides, cholesterol, free fatty acids). Melanocytes transfer melanosomes to keratinocytes to shield nuclei from UV. Thermoregulation uses eccrine sweating (up to about 1-2 L/h) and arteriovenous anastomoses.

did_you_know: Your outer skin layer is replaced about every 4 to 6 weeks.

title: Skeletal system
summary: Bones, cartilage and joints support the body, protect organs, anchor muscles and store minerals.

layers.basics: Your skeleton is a living frame. Bones hold you up, shield the brain and heart, give muscles something to pull on, and make blood cells inside their marrow.
layers.deeper: An adult has about 206 named bones, split into the axial skeleton (skull, spine, rib cage) and the appendicular skeleton (limbs and girdles). Bone is constantly remodeled, and it is the body's main reservoir of calcium and phosphate.
layers.expert: Bone is a composite of type I collagen and carbonated hydroxyapatite. Remodeling couples osteoclast resorption with osteoblast formation under RANKL/OPG, PTH, calcitriol and mechanical loading (Wolff's law). Red marrow produces hematopoietic lineages; yellow marrow stores fat.

did_you_know: Newborns have roughly 270-300 bony elements that fuse down to about 206 in adulthood.

title: Muscular system
summary: Skeletal muscles pull on bones to move the body, hold posture and generate heat.

layers.basics: Muscles work by shortening. You have hundreds of skeletal muscles that you control on purpose, plus heart and smooth muscle that work automatically.
layers.deeper: Skeletal muscles are attached to bones by tendons and act as levers across joints. They can only pull, so they work in opposing pairs (agonist and antagonist). Together they make up about 40% of body mass and produce much of resting body heat.
layers.expert: Force arises from cross-bridge cycling within sarcomeres, controlled by motor-unit recruitment (size principle) and rate coding. Fibers vary from slow oxidative (type I) to fast glycolytic (type IIx), with plasticity under training.

did_you_know: The stapedius in your ear is the smallest skeletal muscle, about 1 mm long.

title: Nervous system
summary: The brain, spinal cord and nerves sense the world, process information and command the body.

layers.basics: Your nervous system is a fast communications network. Neurons send electrical pulses and chemical messages to sense, decide, and move.
layers.deeper: It has a central part (brain and spinal cord) and a peripheral part (nerves, ganglia). The somatic branch handles voluntary movement and sensation; the autonomic branch (sympathetic, parasympathetic, enteric) runs organs automatically.
layers.expert: The CNS contains roughly 86 billion neurons and a similar order of glia. Signaling uses action potentials along axons and chemical or electrical synapses; plasticity (LTP/LTD, structural remodeling) underlies learning. Autonomic output integrates through hypothalamic and brainstem nuclei.

did_you_know: The brain is about 2% of body mass but uses roughly 20% of resting energy.

title: Endocrine system
summary: Glands release hormones into the blood to regulate growth, metabolism, stress and reproduction.

layers.basics: Hormones are chemical messengers. Glands drop them into the blood, and they act slowly but for a long time on far-away targets.
layers.deeper: The endocrine system works through feedback loops such as the hypothalamus-pituitary axes. Hormones are peptides, steroids or amines, and bind receptors on the cell surface or inside cells.
layers.expert: Major axes: HPA (CRH-ACTH-cortisol), HPT (TRH-TSH-T3/T4), HPG, GH-IGF-1. Peptide hormones act through GPCR/RTK second-messenger cascades; steroid and thyroid hormones act through nuclear receptors altering transcription. Pulsatility and circadian rhythm shape effects.

did_you_know: The pituitary gland, the 'master gland', is only about the size of a pea.

title: Cardiovascular system
summary: The heart pumps blood through a closed network of vessels carrying oxygen, nutrients and waste.

layers.basics: Your heart pushes blood around a loop of tubes. The blood delivers oxygen and food to every cell and carries waste away.
layers.deeper: Two circuits operate in series: the pulmonary circuit (right heart to lungs) and the systemic circuit (left heart to the body). About 5 L of blood circulates through roughly 100,000 km of vessels in an adult.
layers.expert: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate (≈ 5 L/min at rest, up to 20-25 L/min in exercise). Mean arterial pressure is regulated by baroreceptors, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and autonomic tone. Capillary exchange follows Starling forces.

did_you_know: The vessel length figure of about 100,000 km is an oft-repeated estimate, and capillaries make up most of it.

title: Lymphatic and immune system
summary: A network of vessels, nodes, organs and cells that returns fluid to blood and defends against infection.

layers.basics: Your immune system hunts invaders. Lymph vessels collect leaked fluid and filter it through lymph nodes, where defender cells check it for germs.
layers.deeper: It has barrier defenses, an innate response (neutrophils, macrophages, complement, inflammation) and an adaptive response (T and B lymphocytes) that remembers pathogens.
layers.expert: Primary lymphoid organs: bone marrow, thymus. Secondary: spleen, lymph nodes, MALT. Adaptive immunity relies on V(D)J recombination for receptor diversity, MHC presentation, clonal selection, and memory formation.

did_you_know: The thymus shrinks throughout adult life and is mostly fat by old age.

title: Respiratory system
summary: Airways and lungs bring oxygen into the blood and remove carbon dioxide.

layers.basics: You breathe to get oxygen. Air flows down the windpipe into the lungs, where oxygen slips into the blood and carbon dioxide leaves.
layers.deeper: Muscles (mainly the diaphragm) expand the chest to draw air in. Gas exchange happens across the thin walls of tiny air sacs called alveoli.
layers.expert: Ventilation is driven by the pressure gradient between atmosphere and alveoli. Gas exchange follows Fick's law across the ≈ 0.5 µm blood-gas barrier; oxygen transport depends on the hemoglobin dissociation curve. Chemoreceptors regulate rate mainly via CO2/H+.

did_you_know: Your lungs' gas-exchange surface is often compared to a tennis court but is closer to a studio apartment, around 70 m².

title: Digestive system
summary: A tube with helper organs that breaks food into nutrients and absorbs them.

layers.basics: Digestion turns your meal into tiny molecules your body can use. Food passes from mouth to stomach to intestines, helped by the liver and pancreas.
layers.deeper: Mechanical churning and chemical digestion by enzymes, acid and bile reduce food to monomers (sugars, amino acids, fatty acids) absorbed mostly in the small intestine. The large intestine reclaims water and hosts gut microbes.
layers.expert: The enteric nervous system and hormones (gastrin, CCK, secretin, GIP, GLP-1) coordinate motility and secretion. Absorption uses brush-border enzymes and transporters (SGLT1, GLUT2/5, PepT1). Hepatic portal blood carries absorbed nutrients to the liver first.

did_you_know: The stomach lining replaces itself every few days because acid and enzymes constantly wear it down.

title: Urinary system
summary: Kidneys filter blood to make urine and keep water, salts and acid-base balance steady.

layers.basics: Your kidneys clean the blood. They remove waste, adjust how much water and salt you keep, and send the extra to the bladder as urine.
layers.deeper: About a fifth of cardiac output passes through the kidneys. The nephrons filter plasma and then reabsorb most water and useful solutes, leaving urine of about 1-2 L per day.
layers.expert: Glomerular filtration rate ≈ 120 mL/min (~180 L/day); >99% reabsorbed. Countercurrent multiplication and ADH set urine concentration up to ≈ 1200 mOsm/kg. Kidneys also produce renin, erythropoietin and activate vitamin D.

did_you_know: Your kidneys filter your entire blood plasma volume about 60 times a day.

title: Reproductive system
summary: Organs that make gametes and hormones and, in females, support a developing embryo.

layers.basics: This system makes sperm or eggs and the hormones that guide sexual development, and it allows a new human to develop.
layers.deeper: Gonads (testes, ovaries) make gametes by meiosis and sex hormones. Ducts, glands and the uterus carry and nurture gametes and the developing embryo.
layers.expert: Gametogenesis is governed by the HPG axis (GnRH, LH, FSH). Testes produce testosterone and sperm continuously after puberty; ovaries release usually one oocyte per cycle under estradiol/progesterone feedback. Meiosis halves chromosome number from 46 to 23.

did_you_know: A human egg is the largest human cell, about 0.1 mm across, just visible to the naked eye.
